questions.question_text: In descriptive studies of psychiatric populations, what is the primary limitation regarding causal inference?

Selection bias is possible but not inherent to the design. Prospective follow-up is not a requirement for descriptive studies—they are complete without it. questions.question_text: In comparing a case-control study to a cohort study investigating the association between occupational stress and major depression, what is the fundamental difference in how subjects are initially identified and grouped?

options.text: Case-control studies identify subjects by exposure history; cohort studies identify by disease status
Case-control studies identify subjects by disease status; cohort studies identify by exposure history
Both designs identify subjects by disease status and then assess exposure
Both designs identify subjects by exposure status and then measure outcomes
Cohort studies cannot identify exposed and non-exposed groups

correct_answer.text: Case-control studies identify subjects by disease status; cohort studies identify by exposure history

questions.explanation: This is a core definitional distinction. Case-control studies start with defined groups separated by disease status (cases vs. controls) and then assess exposure retrospectively. Cohort studies start with exposure status (exposed vs. non-exposed) and follow forward to measure outcomes. This difference determines the temporal direction and measurable statistics (odds ratio vs. relative risk) of each design.

questions.question_text: An experimental study of a new psychotropic medication randomly assigns 100 participants to active drug and 100 to placebo, then measures symptom change over 12 weeks. What distinguishes this design from a cohort study of the same medication in naturalistic practice?

options.text: The experimental study has more statistical power
The experimental study involves deliberate manipulation of exposure through intervention assignment
The experimental study measures outcomes more accurately
The experimental study eliminates selection bias entirely
The experimental study cannot calculate relative risk

questions.explanation: The defining difference between experimental and observational cohort studies is deliberate manipulation of exposure. In experimental studies, the exposure (intervention) is experimentally assigned; in cohort studies, groups are assembled based on naturally occurring exposure differences and observed prospectively. This is the core distinction stated in the source. Neither design eliminates bias, and both can measure relative risk. Accuracy of outcome measurement and statistical power depend on execution, not design type.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of UK adults (aged 16–59) who took an illicit drug in the last year?
questions.explanation: That 1 in 12 adults (8.3%) took an illicit drug in the last year. Of these, frequent users (>once/month) represent 2.8%, with cannabis being the most commonly used at 6.4%. ---

questions.question_text: In a case-control study examining the relationship between antipsychotic medication use and metabolic syndrome, researchers compare the proportion of patients with metabolic syndrome who used antipsychotics to the proportion of controls who used antipsychotics. This comparison is appropriate for calculating which measure of association?

options.text: Relative risk
Odds ratio
Incidence rate
Prevalence ratio
Attributable risk

questions.explanation: Case-control studies cannot measure incidence because both exposure and disease have already occurred; therefore, only odds ratio can be calculated, not relative risk. This is an explicit limitation of case-control designs stated in the source. The cross-product ratio (odds ratio) is the appropriate measure for case-control studies. Relative risk requires knowledge of incidence. Incidence and prevalence ratios also require prospective data.

questions.question_text: What is the critical distinction between an ecological study and an individual-level analytical study examining the relationship between social factors and psychiatric disorder rates?

options.text: Ecological studies use prospective data while individual studies use retrospective data
Ecological studies consider populations as the unit of analysis and assume equal exposure within populations
Ecological studies cannot identify individual risk factors for disease
Ecological studies are always experimental in design
Both B and C

questions.explanation: Ecological studies use populations rather than individuals as the unit of measurement and assume all members of a population are equally exposed and carry the same risk, disregarding within-group differences. This design feature means individual-level conclusions cannot be validly drawn (ecological fallacy). Therefore, individual risk factors cannot be reliably identified from population-level data. Both statements are true and related to the same fundamental limitation of ecological design. Ecological studies are observational, not inherently experimental.

questions.question_text: In a cohort study of psychiatric outcomes, the researcher assembles 500 individuals with recent cannabis use and 500 individuals without cannabis use, following both groups for 10 years. This design choice (comparing exposed vs. non-exposed) reflects which fundamental aspect of cohort studies?

options.text: Subjects are identified and grouped based on their exposure status
Subjects are identified and grouped based on their disease status
Subjects are randomly assigned to receive an intervention
Subjects are selected from a population at a single point in time
Subjects are selected from healthcare records retrospectively

correct_answer.text: Subjects are identified and grouped based on their exposure status

questions.explanation: Cohort studies are defined by grouping subjects based on differences in exposure (exposed vs. non-exposed) and then following them forward to detect outcomes. This is the fundamental design characteristic. Case-control studies group by disease status (cases vs. controls). Experimental studies involve random assignment of intervention. Cross-sectional studies measure at one point in time. Case-control studies use retrospective selection based on disease status.

questions.question_text: Cross-sectional surveys measure the prevalence of a psychiatric symptom cluster in a population at a single point in time. Which statement best describes the strength of this design?

options.text: It can definitively establish causation between risk factors and symptoms
It can measure incidence rates of new psychiatric diagnoses
It can suggest the presence of relationships among variables without establishing causality
It eliminates all selection bias through matching procedures
It is the most efficient design for studying rare psychiatric outcomes

correct_answer.text: It can suggest the presence of relationships among variables without establishing causality

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies are described as being able to suggest the presence of putative relationships among variables, which is their primary strength. However, they cannot establish causality definitively. They measure prevalence (snapshot at one point in time), not incidence. They are called prevalence studies specifically for this reason. They do not eliminate selection bias through matching—matching is a feature of analytical studies like case-control. They are not efficient for rare outcomes because prevalence is too low at any single point in time.
